lines.text: The human body is organized into systems, each with a specialized role. The circulatory system — the heart, blood vessels, and blood — delivers oxygen and nutrients to every cell. The respiratory system, centered on the lungs and airways, handles gas exchange: oxygen in, carbon dioxide out. The digestive system breaks down food into nutrients through the mouth, stomach, and intestines. The nervous system, led by the brain and spinal cord, controls thoughts, movements, and reflexes through a network of nerves. The muscular system provides movement; skeletal muscles attach to bones and contract to produce motion. The skeletal system gives the body structure and protects organs. The immune system defends against disease using white blood cells, antibodies, and lymph nodes. The endocrine system releases hormones from glands like the thyroid, adrenal glands, and pituitary gland to regulate growth, metabolism, and mood. The urinary system filters waste through the kidneys and bladder. The reproductive system enables the creation of new life. The integumentary system — skin, hair, and nails — protects the body from the outside world. Finally, the lymphatic system drains excess fluid and supports immunity. Together, these systems maintain homeostasis — the body's internal balance.

lines.text: English names body systems using adjective + 'system': circulatory, respiratory, digestive, nervous, muscular, skeletal, immune, endocrine, urinary, reproductive, integumentary, lymphatic. Memorize the adjective form.
lines.name: English names body systems using adjective + 'system': circulatory, respiratory, digestive, nervous, muscular, skeletal, immune, endocrine, urinary, reproductive, integumentary, lymphatic. Memorize the adjective form.

lines.text: Doctors say 'cardiovascular' (circulatory), 'pulmonary' (respiratory), 'gastrointestinal' (digestive), 'dermatological' (integumentary). Everyday English prefers the simpler system names.
lines.name: Doctors say 'cardiovascular' (circulatory), 'pulmonary' (respiratory), 'gastrointestinal' (digestive), 'dermatological' (integumentary). Everyday English prefers the simpler system names.

lines.text: English uses body systems as metaphors: 'the nervous system of a company' (communication), 'the circulatory system of a city' (transportation), 'the immune system of democracy' (checks and balances).
lines.name: English uses body systems as metaphors: 'the nervous system of a company' (communication), 'the circulatory system of a city' (transportation), 'the immune system of democracy' (checks and balances).

lines.text: Western medicine treats each system separately (specialist doctors). Holistic approaches (Chinese medicine, Ayurveda) view all systems as interconnected. English has vocabulary for both perspectives.
